prime.problem: Repeatedly taking the smallest item from a changing collection costs a full scan per pop with an unsorted list, or an O(n) shift per insert with a sorted list. At n = 10⁶ either is 10⁶ steps per operation.
prime.fits: Follows the tree cards: a heap is a complete binary tree with no node objects, stored in a list by index arithmetic. The toolkit card gave heapq's costs; this card shows why they hold. Sliding window median and the Fibonacci heap build directly on it.
expect: sift up after push, sift down after pop
negate for a max-heap; lazy deletion for stale entries
Course Schedule III: a max-heap of durations
prime.goal: Explain why push and pop are O(log n) and heapify is O(n), and use a heap to solve problems that only ever need the current smallest or largest (Course Schedule III, Skyline, Rearrange String).

attend: Why is the heap rule enough to put the minimum at index 0, without sorting anything else?
Why does fixing the rule after a push or pop touch only one root-to-leaf path?
Why is heapify O(n) when n pushes are O(n log n)?
In Course Schedule III, why is dropping the longest course taken so far always safe?
Why can't heapq delete or update an item in the middle?

must: Every parent ≤ its children → the root is the minimum → peek is O(1), and the rest stays only loosely ordered, so pushes and pops are cheap
A complete tree in a list has ⌊log₂ n⌋ levels → push appends a leaf and sifts it up; pop moves the last leaf to the root and sifts it down → one path, O(log n) (at most 19 swaps at n = 10⁶)
Heapify sifts down every parent from the bottom up → most nodes sit near the leaves and move a level or two → the total is O(n), cheaper than n pushes

Course Schedule III: take courses by deadline → if days pass the deadline, pop the longest taken so far from a max-heap (−duration) → count stays, days used shrink, later courses can only benefit → O(n log n)
elevated: heapq can only remove the top → updating or deleting a middle item means pushing a new entry and skipping stale ones when they surface (lazy deletion) → the heap can grow beyond the live item count
Ties compare the next tuple field → store (priority, counter, item) when items aren't comparable, as the heapq docs recommend
reference: heappop's leaf-first sift with the right child on ties
the Skyline and Rearrange String example inputs
the exact list [2, 5, 6, 9, 5] vs heapq's [2, 5, 6, 5, 9] after pop

compress.prompt: From memory, draw [1, 2, 6, 5, 5, 9] as a tree, then show one pop step by step and explain in 3 sentences why push, pop and heapify cost what they do.
checklist: pop: return 1, move 9 to the root, swap with the smaller child 2, then 5
each sift walks one path: O(log n)
heapify is O(n) because most nodes are near the bottom
heapq is min-only: store −x or (−priority, …) for a max

retrieve.q: Explain why a heap, unlike a sorted list, gets O(log n) inserts.
answer: a sorted list keeps total order, so an insert shifts every later item: O(n)
a heap keeps only parent ≤ child, so a new leaf only needs to climb its own path
that path is ⌊log₂ n⌋ long in a complete tree

retrieve.q: Dijkstra in Python needs decrease-key, which heapq lacks. What does the standard workaround cost compared with an indexed heap or a Fibonacci heap?
answer: push a duplicate with the smaller distance and skip stale pops
the heap may hold up to E entries: O(E log E) = O(E log V)
an indexed heap does decrease-key in O(log V) but needs a key → index map kept in sync on every swap
a Fibonacci heap makes it O(1) amortized, but with large constants

compare.q: Binary heap vs Fibonacci heap: when does each do its tidying work, and which operation's cost does that laziness change?
answer: the binary heap restores its rule immediately on every push and pop
the Fibonacci heap defers all tidying to extract-min (consolidate)
insert and decrease-key drop from O(log n) to O(1) amortized
extract-min stays O(log n) amortized, with larger constants and 7 fields per node

compare.q: The same sift-down builds a priority queue here and sorts an array in heapsort. What does heapsort do with each popped maximum, and what does it give up compared with merge sort?
answer: heapsort heapifies in O(n), then repeatedly swaps the max to the end and sifts down
in place, O(n log n) worst case
not stable, and its jumps through memory are cache-unfriendly
merge sort is stable but needs O(n) extra memory

predict.q: Run schedule_course on [[3, 2], [4, 3]] (each course is [duration, last day]). Before tracing: how many courses can be taken, and what does the heap do at each step?
predict.answer: 0. Sorted by deadline, the first course needs 3 days by day 2: days = 3 > 2, so it is pushed and immediately popped. The second needs 4 days by day 3: days = 4 > 3, pushed and popped again. Each course is longer than its own deadline, so neither can ever fit.

apply.task: Heapify [5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6] by hand with sift-down, starting at index n // 2 − 1 = 2 and going back to 0. Count the swaps and compare with the six pushes on the card. Then run schedule_course on [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]] and trace the heap.
apply.done: Heapify gives [1, 2, 6, 5, 5, 9] in 4 swaps (9↔6, 2↔1, then 5↔1 and 5↔2), the same list and swap count as the six pushes; the schedule answer is 2 (after the third course days = 6 > 4, so the 3-day course is popped).
apply.hint: At index 0, 5 first swaps with its smaller child 1 and then keeps sinking.
